title: What is Learning - 2
author: Martin Skelton
summary: This early post in the Looking for Learning series separates development from learning. Skelton explains that some neuronal chains are already hardwired through evolution and unfold on their own schedule, so parents and teachers can observe but not accelerate them. He uses the debate over school starting age, seven in some Scandinavian systems versus three or four in the UK, to show that both positions are really arguments about developmental readiness. Learning proper, by contrast, begins once that foundation exists and depends on planned or accidental experiences shaped by culture, choices and relationships. From this he reframes a teacher's job as preparing the best experiences at the right developmental moment, and expands his working definition of learning accordingly, promising a follow-up on energy.
points: Development is the species-wide hardwiring that arrives on its own timetable, while learning is the experience-dependent getting better that adults can plan and support.
Neither deprivation nor expensive toys speeds up development, so patience and observation are the right adult responses in the earliest years.
The school-starting-age dispute is reframed as a disagreement about developmental readiness rather than about learning itself.
A teacher whose focus is learning designs the best repeated experiences for each brain, which is a very different job from the one-size-fits-all sage on the stage.
quotes: For some time, our brains at birth were thought to be a blank slate, waiting to be written on by our lifelong experiences. But some neuronal chains are created before we are born.
It’s her baked-in developmental hardwiring that causes this to happen. We observe it, but we don’t really affect it.
Mostly, we have to wait for these developments to take place. We can’t help our six-month old to walk ahead of some crucial baked-in neuronal chains being formed.

For now, though, the point is a simple one. Both of these arguments about school starting age are framed, often without being clear about it, around the species-wide developmental hardwiring of a young child’s neurons in her brain.

Once this development has happened we can begin to talk about learning as something that can be supported and planned. This kind of learning isn’t ‘natural’ in the sense that developmental learning is because there are choices and attitudes involved.

Obviously, learning happens in schools. Schools are places especially created so that parents and societies can outsource a range of planned experiences for children and students that will help them learn across subjects and areas that our culture believes are important.

A teacher’s job is, at the most appropriate developmental time, to deliberately prepare the best experiences possible in the classroom so that the brain of each child and student builds the maximum number of neuronal constellations it possibly can. The ‘sage on the stage’, one-size fits all traditional teacher is a very, very different being than a teacher whose hedgehog concept is learning.
